additions.title: UK GDPR, Article 39: Tasks of the data protection officer
additions.quote: awareness-raising and training of staff involved in processing operations, and the related audits
additions.why: The nearest binding UK training rule: where an organisation must have a data protection officer, that officer monitors compliance including staff awareness and training. Limits: applies only where a data protection officer is required, covers personal data handling only, and is not an AI literacy duty; the brief's statement that no UK statute sets a general AI literacy duty stands.

additions.title: Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI
additions.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
additions.quote: AI security training shall be tailored to the specific roles and responsibilities of staff members.
additions.why: A UK government code that makes role-based AI training an expected practice, with content reviewed as threats change and all staff kept aware. Limits: voluntary; covers security awareness, not general competence in using AI; the page says government intends to mirror a future ETSI standard.

additions.title: R (Ayinde) v London Borough of Haringey; Al-Haroun v Qatar National Bank [2025] EWHC 1383 (Admin)
additions.publisher: High Court of Justice, King's Bench Division (Divisional Court), via The National Archives Find Case Law
additions.quote: understands and complies with their professional and ethical obligations and their duties to the court if using artificial intelligence
additions.why: A court holding those with leadership responsibilities to account for whether everyone in their organisation understands how to use AI properly, after fictitious AI-generated citations reached the court; it says future hearings will ask whether those responsibilities were met. Limits: concerns the legal profession and duties to the court; England and Wales.

additions.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI): Guidance for Judicial Office Holders
additions.locator: Section 3, part I: Understand AI and its applications
additions.quote: Before using any AI tools, ensure you have a basic understanding of their capabilities and potential limitations.
additions.why: A worked example of baseline literacy set for a whole workforce, including clerks, assistants and support staff: understand limits first, then verify output and take responsibility. Limits: applies to the judiciary only; replaces the April 2025 edition and is likely to be refreshed again.

additions.title: Use of artificial intelligence in government (HC 612, Session 2023-24)
additions.quote: Departments identified a lack of AI skills as a key barrier to adoption of AI in government.
additions.why: Audit evidence that the skills gap is the commonest obstacle: 70% of the 87 government bodies surveyed named difficulty recruiting or retaining staff with AI skills. Limits: public sector; survey in autumn 2023; about specialist skills as much as general staff literacy.

additions.title: Artificial intelligence in UK financial services - 2024
additions.publisher: Bank of England and Financial Conduct Authority
additions.locator: Section 4.5: Non-regulatory constraints to AI adoption
additions.quote: Insufficient talent/access to skills was considered by 25% of firms to be a large constraint
additions.why: Regulators' survey evidence from a heavily regulated sector that skills limit safe adoption; the same survey reports that 46% of firms have only a partial understanding of the AI they use. Limits: financial services only; a voluntary survey of regulated firms; 2024 data.

additions.title: The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking: Self-Reported Reductions in Cognitive Effort and Confidence Effects From a Survey of Knowledge Workers
additions.publisher: Lee, Sarkar, Tankelevitch, Drosos, Rintel, Banks and Wilson; CHI 2025 (author copy hosted by Microsoft Research)
additions.quote: higher confidence in GenAI is associated with less critical thinking, while higher self-confidence is associated with more critical thinking
additions.why: Peer-reviewed conference paper showing why literacy must cover judgement and not only tool use: workers who trust the tool more check it less. Limits: self-reported survey of 319 knowledge workers recruited online (37 resident in the UK); correlation, not cause; authors work for a vendor of AI tools.

additions.title: A Brief AI Literacy Intervention Does Not Significantly Reduce Over-Reliance and Increases Under-Reliance on ChatGPT: A Randomized Study
additions.quote: The intervention did not significantly reduce over-reliance.
additions.why: A randomised test of a short, text-based literacy briefing: it did not reduce acceptance of wrong AI advice and made people reject more correct advice. Supports measuring effectiveness and not attendance. Limits: preprint, not peer reviewed (v2, 18 September 2026); high school students in Estonia, not employees; maths puzzles; abstract only was read.

additions.title: Model Artificial Intelligence Governance Framework, Second Edition
additions.publisher: Infocomm Media Development Authority and Personal Data Protection Commission, Singapore
additions.locator: Internal governance structures and measures, paragraph 3.7, item 2(iv) (printed page 23)
additions.quote: Ensuring relevant staff dealing with AI systems are properly trained.
additions.why: International comparator: Singapore's framework ties training to role, with those working directly with models trained to interpret output and detect bias, and other staff trained to know benefits, risks and limits. Limits: voluntary; Singapore; 2020, before generative AI tools were in general use.

rejected.title: Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (CETS 225)
rejected.reason: HTTP 403 to a plain request (also the treaty page on coe.int). Not bypassed, not read, not cited. No UK government copy of the treaty text was found by search.

rejected.title: Australian Government: Policy for the responsible use of AI in government; Voluntary AI Safety Standard (10 guardrails)
rejected.reason: No response to a plain request (connection timed out, HTTP 0), same for industry.gov.au. Not read, not cited.

rejected.title: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier (Dell'Acqua and others, Harvard Business School Working Paper 24-013)
rejected.reason: HTTP 403 to a plain request. Not bypassed, not read, not cited.

rejected.title: AI Tools in Society: Impacts on Cognitive Offloading and the Future of Critical Thinking (Gerlich, Societies 2025; UK sample)
rejected.reason: HTTP 403 to a plain request. Not read, not cited.

rejected.title: OECD Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence (OECD/LEGAL/0449)
rejected.reason: Page returns a script shell (69 characters of text). Not read. The OECD's own principle page on oecd.ai was readable and is used under workforce impact assessment, where it fits better.

rejected.title: FCA Handbook, SYSC 5.1.1R (competent employees rule)
rejected.reason: Read and relevant, but placed under oversight capability to avoid recording the same passage twice in one domain.

rejected.title: ISO/IEC 42001 and other ISO pages
rejected.reason: iso.org returns HTTP 403 with a browser challenge. Not bypassed.

brief_check: Nothing read contradicts the approved brief. Two points support it: no UK source found sets a general AI literacy duty (UK GDPR Art. 39 is confined to data protection officers), and the one randomised study read (a 2025 preprint on students) found a brief text-only briefing did not reduce over-reliance, which backs 'competence tested, not attendance counted'.
